Clinical Documentation Improvement (CDI)

Making the Chart Say What Actually Happened

Clinical documentation improvement is the discipline of making sure a patient's chart fully and accurately reflects how sick they were and how complex their care actually was. A coder can only code what's written down. If a physician treats a patient for sepsis but only documents "infection," the chart, the code, the DRG and the reimbursement all end up understating what really happened.

CDI closes that gap by reviewing documentation while a patient is still in care, or shortly after, and querying the physician for clarification when something is unclear, incomplete, or inconsistent with the clinical picture. This isn't about adding diagnoses that didn't happen, it's about making sure the ones that did happen are written down clearly enough for coding to capture them correctly.

PMEX's CDI specialists work directly with providers, using a formal, respectful query process, so documentation supports accurate coding, fair reimbursement, and quality metrics that actually reflect the care delivered.

The Physician Query Process

Asking the Right Question, the Right Way

A query is a clarifying question to a physician, never a suggestion of what to write. Every query PMEX sends follows the same compliant structure.

Identify the Gap

Documentation reviewed for vague, incomplete or clinically inconsistent notes.

Draft a Compliant Query

A clarifying, non-leading question is written, with clinical indicators cited.

Physician Response

The provider reviews and responds directly in the chart, in their own words.

Coding Reflects the Update

The clarified documentation flows directly into final coding and DRG assignment.

CDI Program Metrics

Productivity Metrics and Program Success Metrics

A healthy CDI program is measured two ways: how the team is working, and whether that work is actually changing outcomes.

Productivity Metrics

  • •Review rate: share of eligible charts reviewed
  • •Query rate: how often a chart generates a query
  • •Response rate: how many queries get a physician response
  • •Query agreement rate: how often the response supports the query

Program Success Metrics

  • •Case mix index (CMI) trend
  • •CC/MCC capture rate
  • •Severity of illness (SOI) and risk of mortality (ROM) accuracy
  • •Observed-to-expected (O/E) mortality alignment

Clinical Documentation Improvement: Frequently Asked Questions

No. Coding assigns codes to whatever is documented. CDI works before and alongside coding to make sure the documentation itself is complete and accurate enough for coding to capture the full clinical picture.

No. A compliant query only asks the physician to clarify something already suggested by the clinical evidence, and never suggests a specific diagnosis or leads the response. The physician always decides what to write.

A complication or comorbidity (CC) or major complication or comorbidity (MCC) reflects added clinical complexity that affects DRG assignment and reimbursement. If documentation doesn't clearly capture a CC or MCC that was actually present, the DRG understates the true resource intensity of the case.

CDI started as an inpatient MS-DRG discipline, but the same documentation principles apply to outpatient and professional fee charts, particularly for supporting medical necessity and HCC risk-adjustment accuracy.

Most medical necessity denials trace back to documentation that doesn't clearly support the service billed. Fixing that gap at the source, while the patient is still in care, means fewer claims ever reach the point of being denied.
